title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi in Braj, Krishna's colors, sticks in Barsana and petals in Vrindavan. Everyone's the same color today.

Look closely at many images of Shiva, and his throat is a darker blue than the rest of him. It isn't a painting mistake; it's a scar, of a kind. One of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated. And one story people tell about Maha Shivaratri is how his throat got that color: a moment when the whole universe nearly ended, and one god drank the danger so everyone else could live.
screen: `A BLUE THROAT.` → `NILAKANTHA.` → `THE NIGHT HE DRANK THE DANGER.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its eighth book. The gods and the demons, usually enemies, agree to work together for once. They want amrita, the nectar of immortality, at the bottom of the ocean of milk. So they churn the ocean, the samudra manthan, with the mountain Mandara as the churning stick and the great serpent Vasuki as the rope, gods pulling one end, demons the other. But the first thing that rises isn't nectar. It's poison: Halahala, so strong its fumes spread in every direction and begin to burn the worlds. Gods, demons, every creature, run to Shiva. The text says Shiva looks on them with compassion, and his wife, the Goddess, agrees. He gathers the poison in his palm and drinks it. And in the telling many know, he holds it in his throat. He doesn't swallow it all the way down, where it would destroy him and the world inside him, and he doesn't spit it out, where it would destroy everyone else. He keeps it right there, and his throat turns blue. Some devotees connect Shivaratri to that night: the gods stayed awake, singing to Shiva, so the poison wouldn't overcome him. It's one explanation among several, but it fits the vigil. The night isn't only about staying up. It's about keeping someone company while they hold something hard.
screen: `THE CHURNING OF THE OCEAN.` · `FIRST, NOT NECTAR, BUT POISON.` · `SHIVA DRINKS IT.` · `HELD IN THE THROAT: NILAKANTHA.` · then, large: `KEEP COMPANY WITH THE ONE WHO HOLDS IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're holding that you can't swallow and can't spit out: a worry, a hard conversation coming, a grief. Don't push it down or away; let it sit in the throat or the chest while you breathe around it. Keep it company, the way the gods kept Shiva company.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, the blue-throated one, who held the world's poison so others could live.
Your line: stay awake for what matters. Tomorrow, a thread tied during a losing war. Day six hundred eighty-two, done.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus keep vigil at Shiva temples through the night, chanting and offering water, milk and bilva leaves to the lingam; some connect the night with Shiva drinking the poison from the churned ocean.

original.note: Sanskrit nīla (blue) + kaṇṭha (throat): Shiva, the blue-throated.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shiva's blue throat is just how he's painted.
what it means: it's the mark of the poison he held to save the worlds.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata Purana's eighth book tells Shiva drinking the halahala at the churning of the ocean; the link to Shivaratri's vigil is one of several explanations people give.

chat.says: Why is Shiva's throat always painted blue?
options: He drank the poison from the churned ocean and held it in his throat to save everyone.
It's from a battle wound a demon gave him during the churning of the ocean.
It's only an artist's choice of color, with no story behind it.
chat.meaning: In the Bhagavata, Shiva drinks the halahala to save every creature; in the telling many know, he holds it in his throat, which turns blue.
